### P036 -- 2026-09-13 18:54 -- PARTLY

> You can also see in the two images, I've selected one chunk further up (green) and one chunk way further down (green also). I would suspect one piece of evidence to hold onto here is the fact that these chunks, once stripped to text only, would affect the partitioning count to be more conservative with its sub-chunking problems, which may also help with deduplication as well. Perhaps we could inform dedup with intra-embedding metrics on a DOM page? And for that matter, an algorithm that can also intelligently sinkhorn/anneal the chunks that are actually the same thing, but just outside of our existing metrics and heuristics that constrain the context windows. I would suggest the context windows aren't necessarily hard constraints, but obviously necessary and worth staging first with embedding dedup and merging second, since then we can begin with an appropriate window that is in fact still a subset of the max context window (remember, we chose 256 because of the hit@1). Perhaps this is where DBSCAN comes in, but to a more nearest-neighbors feature-metric aggregation kind of thing. I've also attached a couple more images of the same example chunk; most of the tokens are, in fact, link text that does not count towards the overall chunk window limit, since this new limit assumes only the bare text (alts, etc). Worth consideration to build and test for. 
>
> One thing to mention about the dedup; it should happen over the db-side representation of the aggregate DOM chunks first and foremost since we're still getting duplicate chunks in a  lot of cases currently. The embedding-side aggregation (dbscan etc) would enable a more intelligent partitioning of per-page chunks that begins recursively, and then bridges to embeddings with DBSCAN. Since we are focused on coarse-to-fine localized to shadow DOMs, we're not doing this for all shadow DOMs at a time, so we can make this a second stage to the *chunking* process which is not necessarily a completely new thing that happens outside of the scanning process itself. We can likely get away with DBSCAN on the quantized semantic chunks only, since frequency vectors are not dimension efficient and simply are there for the fine-grained preservation in retrieval, while larger-scale chunking and dedup merges can happen as a second stage after our 256 vectorization. We can keep the original 256-style chunks and their embeddings underneath, but a merge layer would be what actually indexes the overall high-level chunks that can then still be retrieved as 256, but represented, structured, and presented as the similarity-merged ones. There would have to be some careful determination between what counts as more or less 'exact' duplicates and what counts as 'should be merged as a larger chunk'. I don't think substring matching would work as well here, so it would have to be a careful metric thing.
